title: W.P No. 518-A of 2025 Hazir Khan and others  Vs  Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
text:
1
JUDGMENT SHEET
PESHAWAR HIGH COURT
ABBOTTABAD BENCH
(Judicial Department)
W.P. No.518-A/2025
Hazir Khan and others.
(Petitioner/s)
VS
Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Chief
Secretary, Peshawar and others.
(Respondent/s)
Present: Mr. Ajmal Khan Tahirkheli, Advocate, for
petitioner.
Mr. Asim Shamshad, Advocate, Legal
Advisor for Excise and Taxation Department
alongwith Mr. Mehboob Elahi and
Mr. Abdul Hafeez (Excise Inspectors).
Mr. Sheikh Abid Ali, Advocate, for
respondent No. 6
Date of hearing: 02.06.2026
JUDGMENT
AURANGZEB, J.- Through this consolidated judgment,
we propose to decide the instant writ petition as well as
connected Constitutional Petitions bearing Nos. 924-
A/2022, 520-A/2025, 595-A/2025, 820-A/2025, 821-
A/2025, 827-A/2025, 878-A/2025, 920-A/2025 and 984-
A/2025, as all these petitions involve common questions of
law and fact relating to the levy, assessment and recovery
of Urban Immovable Property Tax under the provisions of
the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Urban Immovable Property Tax
2
Act, 1958, and, therefore, can conveniently be disposed of
through a single judgment.
2. In the instant writ petition, the petitioners
have averred that they are residents of Village Khalo,
Tehsil Ghazi, District Haripur, and are owners of various
immovable properties, including shops and commercial
buildings situated within the said locality. According to the
petitioners, Village Khalo falls within a rural area and has
never been declared an urban area by the Government
under Section 3 of the Urban Immovable Property Tax
Act, 1958. It has further been pleaded that respondent
No.6/Tehsil Municipal Administration issued notices dated
23.04.2025 and 24.04.2025 requiring the petitioners to pay
Urban Immovable Property Tax in respect of their
properties. Aggrieved by the issuance of the said notices,
the petitioners preferred appeals on 28.04.2025 before
respondent No.5 under Section 10 of the Urban Immovable
Property Tax Act, 1958. It is their grievance that despite
the pendency of the said appeals, respondent No.5 failed to
decide the same, while respondent No.4 proceeded further
with the recovery proceedings and issued additional
notices for recovery of Urban Immovable Property Tax. In
these circumstances, the petitioners have invoked the
constitutional jurisdiction of this Court and seek
declaration of the impugned notices as being without
lawful authority and of no legal effect.
3
3. In Constitutional Petition No.924-A/2022,
the petitioner has challenged demand notice dated
29.07.2022 issued by respondent No.3 under Rules 15(4)
and 15(5) of the West Pakistan Urban Immovable Property
Tax Rules, 1958, read with the relevant provisions of the
West Pakistan Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958,
whereby an amount of Rs.11,51,540/- was demanded from
the petitioner on account of Urban Immovable Property
Tax. The petitioner contends that the building in question
does not fall within the municipal limits of respondent
No.4 and, therefore, is not liable to the payment of Urban
Immovable Property Tax under the applicable statutory
framework. On the basis of the aforesaid assertions, the
petitioner seeks declaration that the impugned demand
notice has been issued without lawful authority and is
liable to be set aside.
4. In Constitutional Petition No.520-A/2025,
the petitioners have asserted that they are affectees of the
Tarbela Dam Project and, after displacement from their
ancestral villages, were rehabilitated in Khalabat
Township. It has been pleaded that the Tarbela Dam
Project was undertaken as a national project for generation
of hydroelectric power and that, in recognition of the
hardships suffered by the displaced inhabitants, the
Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa declared Khalabat
Township a “weak town” vide letter No. SOR(Dir)4-
17/2001-Haripur dated 01.09.2007, whereunder the
4
residents of the township were exempted from payment of
drinking water charges. It has further been averred that
additional governmental assistance and funds were
provided from time to time for the welfare of the affectees.
The petitioners contend that the impugned PT-10 and PT-
11 notices have been issued without lawful authority and,
therefore, seek their annulment through the exercise of
constitutional jurisdiction.
5. In Constitutional Petition No.595-A/2025,
the petitioner claims to be the owner of immovable
property situated in Village Shah Muhammad and contends
that respondent No.5 issued a final notice dated 28.05.2025
under the Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958,
without first issuing any assessment notice, show-cause
notice or personal intimation as allegedly required by law.
The petitioner maintains that the impugned action is
violative of due process and contrary to the mandatory
procedure prescribed under the relevant statutory
provisions. Consequently, he seeks declaration that the
impugned notice is illegal, void and without lawful
authority.
6. Constitutional Petition No.820-A/2025 has
been filed by petitioners who also claim to be affectees of
the Tarbela Dam Project. According to them, the
controversy involved in their petition is identical to that
raised in Constitutional Petition No.520-A/2025. They
have challenged the impugned PT-10 and PT-11 notices on
5
the ground that the same have been issued without lawful
authority and are liable to be set aside.
7. Likewise, in Constitutional Petition No.821-
A/2025, the petitioners have questioned the legality of the
impugned PT-10 and PT-11 notices. Their case is founded
upon the assertion that they too are affectees of the Tarbela
Dam Project and stand on the same footing as the
petitioners in Constitutional Petition No.520-A/2025. They
have, therefore, sought identical relief.
8. Constitutional Petition No.827-A/2025 has
also been instituted by persons claiming to be affectees of
the Tarbela Dam Project. The factual matrix set up therein
is substantially the same as that pleaded in Constitutional
Petition No.520-A/2025. The petitioners challenge the
impugned PT-10 and PT-11 notices as having been issued
without lawful authority and seek their annulment.
9. In Constitutional Petition No.878-A/2025,
the petitioner asserts ownership of immovable property
situated in Village Jolian, District Haripur. It has been
pleaded that respondent No.4 issued notice dated
11.02.2025 under the Urban Immovable Property Tax Act,
1958 without prior assessment proceedings, notice or
personal intimation. It is further alleged that a reminder
dated 10.03.2025 was subsequently issued without
compliance with the procedure prescribed by law. The
petitioner contends that the impugned notices are void ab
initio and liable to be struck down.
6
10. In Constitutional Petition No.920-A/2025,
the petitioners have challenged the impugned notices and
PT-11 forms on the ground that they are affectees of the
Tarbela Dam Project and that their case is fully covered by
the controversy involved in Constitutional Petition No.520-
A/2025. They seek the same relief as prayed for in the
connected petitions.
11. In Constitutional Petition No.984-A/2025,
the petitioner has averred that he resides within the
territorial limits of Tehsil Municipal Administration Baffa
Pakhal. According to the petitioner, respondent No.2
issued the impugned notifications whereby various
localities within the territorial jurisdiction of Tehsil
Municipal Administration Baffa Pakhal were declared
rating areas for the purpose of levy and recovery of Urban
Immovable Property Tax. The petitioner has questioned
the legality and constitutional validity of the said
proceedings and seeks declaration that the final notice
dated 27.08.2024, along with the consequential recovery
notices issued on the same date, are without lawful
authority and of no legal effect.
12. Upon issuance of notices in the aforesaid
petitions, the respondents entered appearance and
submitted para-wise comments. The respective pleadings
of the parties, along with the relevant record produced
before the Court, form part of the case file and have been
carefully examined.
7
13. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
petitioners, the learned Legal Advisor for the Excise and
Taxation Department, the learned Additional Advocate
General and the learned counsel representing the private
respondents were heard at considerable length. The record
has also been perused with their able assistance.
14. Before adverting to the merits of the
controversy, it would be advantageous to observe that
issues relating to the levy, assessment and recovery of
Urban Immovable Property Tax under the Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958
have repeatedly engaged the attention of this Court. In
particular, this Court had the occasion to examine the
statutory framework governing Urban Immovable Property
Tax, the concept of rating areas, the powers of local
governments and the Excise and Taxation Department, as
well as the effect of alternate statutory remedies available
under the law in M/s Askari Cement Limited through
Authorized Representative/Company Secretary Brig. Riaz
Ahmed Gondal (Retd.) v. Government of Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa through Chief Secretary and others (W.P.
No.371-P/2021) and connected matters. Since the
controversy raised in the present and connected petitions
substantially overlaps with the issues already considered in
the aforesaid judgment, it would be appropriate to first
examine the legal principles laid down therein.
8
15. At this juncture, it would be advantageous to
refer to the findings recorded by this Court in paragraph
No. 51 of the judgment rendered in W.P. No. 371-P/2021
titled “M/s Askari Cement Limited through Authorized
Representative/Company Secretary Brig. Riaz Ahmed
Gondal (Retd.) versus Government of Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa through its Chief Secretary and others”,
wherein the following legal conclusions were
arrived at:-
51. In view of what has been stated above, this as
well as the connected petitions are disposed of in the
following manner:
i. We declare that through section 44 of the
Act of 2013, the entire tehsil has become a
rating area for the purpose of charging
and collection of UIP Tax under the
enabling provisions of the Act of 1958.
ii. The industrial building is subject to the
imposition of UIP Tax as provided in the
preceding para.
iii. All the notifications as mentioned in Para-
42 of this petition under section 120A of
the Act of 2013 declaring certain
territory/area as a rating area are illegal
and without lawful authority.
iv. In the case of Lucky Cement, the
respondents are directed to re-assess the
liability of the petitioner Company strictly
in accordance with the directions of the
Apex Court in the case of Lucky Cement”.
16. Having given anxious consideration to the
submissions advanced at the Bar, examined the pleadings
of the parties and perused the relevant statutory provisions,
this Court is of the considered view that the controversy
involved in the present and connected petitions does not
require any reconsideration of the legal proposition already
settled in M/s Askari Cement Limited (supra), namely that,
9
by virtue of Section 44(1) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Local Government Act, 2013, every tehsil constitutes a
rating area for the purposes of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958. Likewise, the
determination of these petitions does not hinge upon
whether the properties owned by the petitioners are
situated in urban or rural localities. The principal question
requiring adjudication is whether the mandatory statutory
requirements envisaged under Sections 42 and 44 of the
Act of 2013 were duly complied with before the levy,
assessment and recovery of Urban Immovable Property
Tax were undertaken. Since resolution of this controversy
necessarily depends upon the scope, effect and interplay of
the relevant provisions governing rating areas and
determination of tax rates, it would be advantageous to
examine the statutory scheme embodied in Section 44 of
the Act of 2013, which is reproduced hereunder for facility
of reference;
44. Rating Areas and Property Tax--- (1) On
commencement of this Act, every tehsil shall be rating area
within the meaning of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Urban
Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958 (W.P. Act V of 1958).
(2) The rate of property tax in an area within a tehsil shall
be subject to approval of respective tehsil council:
Provided that in the areas within a tehsil where rate has not
been determined, the areas shall be deemed to be exempted
from property tax till determination of the rate.
(3) Unless varied under sub-section (2) above, the existing
rates in the areas within a tehsil shall remain in force.
Explanation--- For the purpose of this section the “rate”
shall mean the tax leviable under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Urban Immovable Properly Tax Act, 1958 (W.P. Act V of
1958).
10
17. A plain reading of Section 44 demonstrates
that the Legislature has enacted a comprehensive statutory
framework governing the levy, determination and recovery
of Urban Immovable Property Tax. Under sub-section (1),
every tehsil is declared to be a rating area within the
meaning of the Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1958.
Sub-section (2) further mandates that the rate of property
tax applicable within any area of a tehsil shall be subject to
the approval of the respective Tehsil Council. The proviso
appended thereto assumes particular significance, as it
expressly provides that where no rate has been determined,
the area concerned shall be deemed exempt from property
tax until such determination is made. Sub-section (3), in
turn, preserves continuity by stipulating that the existing
rates shall remain in force unless varied in accordance with
sub-section (2). When construed as a whole, Section 44
delineates not only the territorial application of the tax but
also the statutory mechanism through which the applicable
rates are to be lawfully determined, approved and enforced.
18. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
respondents contended that, by virtue of sub-section (3) of
Section 44, the rates prevailing under the previous local
government regime continued automatically and remained
enforceable, with the result that no fresh determination or
approval by the respective Tehsil Council was required.
Although the submission appears attractive at first glance,
it does not withstand close scrutiny. Acceptance of such an
11
interpretation would substantially undermine, if not
altogether render redundant, both sub-section (2) and the
proviso appended thereto. It is a settled principle of
statutory interpretation that every provision enacted by the
Legislature must, as far as possible, be assigned meaning
and effect, and that no part of a statute should be construed
in a manner that renders it superfluous, nugatory or devoid
of practical significance. A construction which nullifies the
express requirement of approval by the Tehsil Council or
renders the deeming exemption contained in the proviso
ineffective cannot, therefore, be regarded as a permissible
interpretation of Section 44.
19. Section 44 must be construed as a cohesive
and integrated statutory scheme, with each of its
components being assigned its due meaning and effect.
Sub-section (2) unequivocally designates the Tehsil
Council as the competent authority for the determination
and approval of the applicable rate of property tax. The
proviso appended thereto further prescribes the legal
consequence flowing from the absence of such
determination, namely, that the area concerned shall be
deemed exempt from property tax until the rate is lawfully
determined. Sub-section (3), when read in harmony with
the preceding provisions, merely preserves continuity in
respect of rates already lawfully approved, determined or
operative under the existing legal framework and obviates
the necessity of repeated legislative or administrative
12
action. It cannot be construed in isolation or interpreted in
a manner that defeats the legislative mandate embodied in
sub-section (2), renders the role of the Tehsil Council
redundant, or nullifies the statutory exemption expressly
created by the proviso. Such a construction alone gives
meaningful effect to every part of Section 44 and preserves
the internal coherence of the statutory scheme enacted by
the Legislature.
20. Particular significance attaches to the
expression “shall be deemed to be exempt” employed by
the Legislature in the proviso to Section 44(2). It is a
settled principle of law that where the Legislature creates a
legal fiction, the Court is under a duty to give full effect to
the fiction so created and to carry it to its logical and
inevitable conclusion. Once the Legislature has expressly
declared that an area shall be deemed exempt from
property tax until the applicable rate is determined, such
declaration cannot be ignored, diluted or rendered
ineffective through a process of interpretation. The
statutory exemption embodied in the proviso continues to
operate with full force unless and until the rate is lawfully
determined and approved by the authority designated under
the statute. The necessary consequence, therefore, is that in
the absence of a valid determination or approval of rates by
the competent authority, no enforceable liability to Urban
Immovable Property Tax can arise, nor can any
13
assessment, demand or recovery proceedings be sustained
in law.
21. Before proceeding further, it would be
advantageous to address another important aspect of the
controversy which surfaced during the course of
arguments, namely, the nature, scope and legal effect of
the powers conferred upon local governments under the
constitutional and statutory framework governing local
taxation. Since a substantial part of the respondents’ case
rests upon the authority purportedly exercised by
administrative functionaries in matters relating to the
determination and approval of property tax rates, it
becomes necessary to examine whether such powers are
administrative in character or whether they partake of a
legislative or quasi-legislative nature under the scheme of
the Constitution and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local
Government Act, 2013.
22. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
respondents contended that Article 140-A of the
Constitution merely envisages the devolution of political,
administrative and financial responsibility to local
governments and does not confer upon them any
legislative authority in the constitutional sense. Proceeding
on this premise, it was argued that the determination or
approval of rates under Sections 42 and 44 of the Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa Local Government Act, 2013 constitutes a
purely administrative function and, therefore, does not
14
require exercise by an elected local council. According to
the respondents, the powers relating to approval or
determination of property tax rates could validly be
exercised by administrative functionaries acting under the
statutory framework governing local governments. The
submission, therefore, necessitates an examination of the
nature and character of the powers entrusted under
Sections 42 and 44 of the Act of 2013 and the
constitutional status of local governments in matters
pertaining to taxation.
23. We are unable to subscribe to such a broad
proposition. It is undoubtedly correct that local
governments do not enjoy plenary legislative competence
comparable to that vested in Parliament or the Provincial
Assemblies. However, it does not follow that they are
entirely devoid of legislative or quasi-legislative authority.
The distinction between primary legislation and delegated
legislation is now firmly embedded in constitutional and
administrative jurisprudence. While local governments
cannot enact laws in the constitutional sense, they may
validly exercise delegated, subordinate or quasi-legislative
powers where such authority has expressly been conferred
upon them by the Legislature. Indeed, where a statute
entrusts a local government institution with the authority to
determine rates, impose taxes, frame bye-laws or regulate
matters of general application within its jurisdiction, the
exercise of such authority transcends the realm of purely
15
administrative action and assumes a legislative or quasi-
legislative character. The correctness of the respondents’
contention must, therefore, be examined in the light of
these well-settled principles.
24. In Rizwan Zaka Gill versus Government of
Punjab (PLD 2015 Lahore 28), the Lahore High Court
observed that local governments do not possess legislative
powers in the same manner as federal or provincial
legislatures. Those observations, however, were rendered
in the context of the constitutional status, composition and
electoral structure of local government institutions and
were not intended to negate every form of delegated or
subordinate legislative authority conferred upon such
bodies by statute. The judgment, therefore, cannot be read
as laying down an absolute proposition that local
governments are incapable of exercising powers of a
legislative or quasi-legislative nature where the Legislature
has expressly entrusted them with such functions. Properly
understood, the decision merely recognizes the distinction
between plenary legislative competence, which vests in
Parliament and the Provincial Assemblies, and delegated
legislative authority, which may validly be exercised by
local government institutions within the limits prescribed
by law.
25. Conversely, in All Pakistan Textile Mills
Association versus Province of Sindh (2004 YLR 192),
the Sindh High Court recognized that although taxation is
16
essentially a legislative function, the Legislature may
authorize local councils to impose taxes subject to
conditions prescribed by law. Likewise, the august
Supreme Court of Pakistan in Province of Punjab versus
Market Committee, Okara (2011 SCMR 1856) identified
the power to frame bye-laws, impose taxes and administer
local funds as essential attributes of a local authority. Such
powers, though not legislative in the plenary constitutional
sense, nevertheless possess a delegated or quasi-legislative
character.
26. The legal position emerging from the
foregoing authorities is that, although local governments
do not possess independent legislative competence, the
exercise of powers relating to the determination of taxes,
rates, fees or other matters of general application assumes
a delegated or quasi-legislative character where such
authority has been entrusted by the Legislature. The
determination of rates under Section 44(2) of the Act of
2013 squarely falls within this category, as it directly
affects the proprietary and fiscal rights of persons situated
within the relevant territorial jurisdiction.
27. It is, therefore, not possible to characterize
the function entrusted under Section 44(2) as a purely
administrative act. The determination or approval of rates
is a normative exercise affecting an entire class of
taxpayers and, therefore, possesses a legislative or, at the
very least, a quasi-legislative character. Such authority
17
must, unless the statute expressly provides otherwise, be
exercised by the institution designated by the Legislature
itself.
28. Support for this interpretation may also be
drawn from the recent judgment of the Lahore High Court
in Mushtaq Ahmad and others versus Government of
Punjab etc. (2025 LHC 7814), wherein pari materia
provisions relating to rating areas and property taxation
were examined. The Lahore High Court held that
legislative declarations contained in local government
enactments were sufficient to constitute rating areas, while
continuity clauses were intended to preserve taxation in
areas already subjected to property tax under the previous
statutory regime.
29. The significance of the aforesaid judgment
lies in its recognition that legislative declarations relating
to rating areas and provisions governing the determination
of rates perform distinct functions within the statutory
scheme. The declaration of a territory as a rating area does
not, by itself, determine the applicability, extent or
enforceability of tax liability. The provisions relating to the
determination of rates must, therefore, be given
independent and meaningful effect.
30. In the present case, the controversy does not
revolve around whether the petitioners’ localities form part
of a rating area. That issue stands settled by Section 44(1)
of the Act of 2013 as well as by the judgment rendered by
18
this Court in Askari Cement Limited. The real question
requiring determination is whether the mandatory
requirements embodied in Sections 42(2) and 44(2) of the
Act were complied with before the impugned assessments
and recovery proceedings were initiated.
31. The proviso appended to Section 44(2)
assumes decisive importance in this regard. The
Legislature has expressly provided that where no rate has
been determined, the area concerned shall be deemed
exempt from property tax until such determination is made.
It is a settled principle that a legal fiction created by statute
must be given its full and logical effect. Consequently,
unless rates are lawfully determined by the competent
authority designated by the Legislature, the statutory
exemption continues to operate and no enforceable liability
to property tax can arise.
32. The interpretation advanced by the
respondents would effectively render both the proviso to
Section 44(2) and the requirement of approval by the
Tehsil Council redundant. If historical rates were
automatically enforceable throughout every locality within
a tehsil irrespective of whether the competent council had
ever exercised its statutory authority, there would have
been no necessity for the Legislature to incorporate the
deeming exemption contained in the proviso. Such a
construction would offend the settled principle of statutory
interpretation that every provision enacted by the
19
Legislature must be assigned meaning and effect, and that
no part of a statute should be treated as superfluous,
redundant or without purpose.
33. The only interpretation that harmonizes all
components of Section 44 is that sub-section (1) declares
every tehsil to be a rating area; sub-section (2) entrusts the
determination of rates to the competent Tehsil Council; the
proviso grants statutory exemption where no rate has been
determined; and sub-section (3) preserves continuity only
in respect of rates already lawfully operative in areas
previously subjected to Urban Immovable Property Tax.
Each provision thus operates within its own sphere without
nullifying or rendering redundant the others.
34. The above interpretation receives further
support from Section 42(2) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Local Government Act, 2013, which expressly provides
that no tax shall be levied without prior publication of the
proposal, invitation and consideration of objections, and
approval of the respective local council. These
requirements are not mere procedural formalities; rather,
they constitute substantive safeguards incorporated by the
Legislature to ensure transparency, accountability and
public participation in matters of local taxation. The
statutory scheme, therefore, entrusts taxation decisions to
representative local institutions and not to executive
functionaries acting in their administrative capacity.
20
35. It may further be observed that the functions
assigned to Tehsil Councils under the Act of 2013 include
the approval of taxes, fines and penalties. Such powers are
legislative and financial in nature. Taxation directly affects
the proprietary rights and financial obligations of citizens
and, therefore, cannot be equated with routine
administrative functions. The requirement of approval by
an elected local council reflects the legislative intent that
taxation decisions should emanate from representative
institutions possessing democratic legitimacy and
accountability.
36. Learned counsel for the respondents, assisted
by the learned Additional Advocate General, however
contended that by virtue of Section 120-A of the Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa Local Government Act, 2013, as amended
from time to time, the powers exercisable by the Tehsil
Council stood vested in the authorized officers during the
period when elected local councils were not functional.
Reliance in this regard was placed upon Notification
No.9541/TMA(H) dated 23.06.2021 and Government
Notification No.SOG/LG/7-12/LG/2019 dated 04.09.2019.
According to the respondents, the Tehsil Municipal
Officer/Authorized Officer was competent to determine
and notify rates for Urban Immovable Property Tax and,
therefore, the impugned notifications were lawfully issued.
Since this contention goes to the root of the controversy, it
21
would be advantageous to reproduce Section 120-A of the
Act of 2013 in its original as well as amended form.
Insertion of section 120-A by way of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2019 ( the first
amendment);
120-A Dissolution of Local Government
(1)
………………………………………………………………………….
(2) The Department shall authorize officers to perform
administrative functions of respective Nazimeen till the
installation of local government under this Act.
(3) All Administrative actions required for giving effect to the
provisions of this Act and transition to the local government
system set up thereunder shall be completed within six months
of the commencement of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local
Government (Amendment) Act, 2019.
Amendments brought by way of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local
Government (Second Amendment) Act, 2019 (The Second
Amendment);
Amendment of section 120-A of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Act
No. XXVIII of 2013.... In the said Act, in section 120-A, in sub-
section (2), after the words "respective Nazimeen" the words
and commas "and also to exercise the powers of their
respective councils and Naib Nazimeen, respectively, under
this Act and rules" shall be inserted."
37. The aforesaid contention, in our considered
view, is devoid of substance. Section 120-A was
introduced as a transitional provision following the
dissolution of local governments and was intended to
ensure continuity in the administration of local affairs
during the interregnum. Even after its subsequent
amendment, the provision cannot be construed as
converting unelected executive officers into substitute
local councils empowered to exercise legislative or fiscal
functions expressly vested by law in representative
institutions.
38. The distinction between administrative
powers, on the one hand, and legislative and financial
powers, on the other, is fundamental and cannot be
overlooked. Article 140-A of the Constitution envisages a
22
democratic local government system vested with political,
administrative and financial responsibility. The power to
levy, approve or determine taxes is essentially legislative
and financial in character and has been expressly entrusted
by statute to elected local councils. Such power directly
affects the proprietary and fiscal rights of citizens and,
therefore, cannot be presumed to have been delegated or
transferred to executive officers in the absence of clear and
unequivocal legislative authorization. The law laid down
by this Court in Muhammad Tahir and others v.
Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and others (PLD
2021 Peshawar 171) fully supports this proposition and
leaves no room for doubt that Section 120-A cannot be
construed so broadly as to authorize administrative officers
to exercise legislative or financial powers specifically
reserved for elected local councils. The relevant
observations are reproduced hereunder:
“Vesting of administrative powers in officers with the
powers of Tehsil or District Councils with full authority
to perform its functions and discharge duties of such
representative bodies would go against the very purpose
of enactment of the Act. It would also go in contrast with
mandate of Article 140-A of the Constitution. A provision
of an Act inserted through an amendment cannot be
construed in a way so as to wipe out the entire Act,
unless the legislature by express words or necessary
intendment intends to give such an effect to the newly
provided law. For empowering the administrative
officers to perform functions of the elected and
representative bodies of Tehsil and District Councils all
the respective sections of the Act providing for the
authority, establishment, functions and composition
would be required to be amended suitably for the
purpose. Even then it would be seen whether such
amendments may be brought during existence of the
mandate of Article 140-A of the Constitution or not.
Without bringing such amendments merely adding the
words "also to exercise the power of their respective
councils and Naib Nazimeen" by way of the amending
23
Act cannot be construed to be having an effect of
substitution of all the elected bodies with the respective
authorized officers by deeming such officers substituted
for such council in all the relevant provisions of the Act.
Section 120-A was inserted by way of the First
Amendment brought in the Local Government Act 2013.
Said section was further amended vide the Second
Amendment of same year i.e. 201.9 by the legislature
with a particular purpose. The purpose had not been
more than authorizing the worthy administrative officers
to perform day to day affairs of the local government.
While construing said provision of law the literal
construction would not solve the riddle but a purposive
construction would have to be adopted. While adopting
the purposive construction the newly inserted provisions
had to be read with the whole scheme, purpose and
objects of the Local Government Act 2013. Hon'ble
Supreme Court of Pakistan while giving its judgment in
the case of "Rana Aamer Raza v. Doctor Minhaj Ahmad
Khan" reported as 2012 SCMR 6 has held that the
Supreme Court had to place a purposive construction on
the provisions of the Constitution so as to make it a living
document. It was also observed that while construing a
statute a court has to keep in mind the statement of
reasons and objects given therein, the statement of
objects given in other laws, in pari materia to the one
under consideration as well as the mandate of the
relevant constitutional provisions. Relevant part of
observations of the Hon'ble Court is reproduced
hereunder for ready reference;
The construction as suggested by learned Astt:
A.G, if placed on the provisions of section 120-A would
not only have the effect of implied repeal of other
provisions of the Local Government Act, but it would
also go in contrast with the mandate of Article 140-A of
the Constitution. Vesting powers of the administrative
officers under section 120-A, cannot be construed to be
for any other purpose than running the day to day
affairs, at the time of transition from one local
government to another. Their role may be compared with
and found analogous to the functionaries of a caretaker
government, about whom Hon'ble Supreme Court of
Pakistan had laid down the law that their mandate
cannot be construed beyond running of the day to day
affairs of the government, while giving its judgment in
the case of "Khawaia Muhammad Asif v. Federation of
Pakistan and others" reported as 2013 SCMR 1205.
Relevant part of observations of the august Court is
reproduced hereunder for ready reference;
"Essentially, according to the settled and
accepted norms/ practice, the Caretaker Government
(Prime Minister and Cabinet) is required to perform its
functions to attend to the day-to-day matters, which are
necessary to run the affairs of the State and also to watch
the national interests, etc., in any eventuality in absence
of an elected Government, and such Government is not
authorized to make decisions/appointments having effect
on the working/policies of the future Government, which
is likely to take over after the elections. Apart from
providing assistance to the Election Commission in
organizing free, fair, honest and just elections in the
24
country, it is not vested with the authority to take
decisions concerning the affairs of the Government,
which are bound to pre-empt the scope and sphere of
activity, powers and jurisdiction of an elected
Government. A Caretaker Government possesses limited
powers and authority particularly in view of the fact that
when it is appointed, there is no National Assembly in
place and thus the all important aspect of accountability
is absent. Further, the exercise of complete powers by the
Caretaker Government goes against the doctrine of
separation of powers which is the lifeline of any vibrant
democracy. As noted earlier, the absence of legislature
results in lack of checks and balances. The Caretaker
Government also lacks the mandate of the majority of
people, which is to be acquired by elected government
through the general elections. Therefore, if a Caretaker
Government is allowed to exercise complete powers
available to an elected Government, it may make an
attempt to continue to remain in office for a longer
period of time or may take such decisions which may
cause problems for the future elected government."
39. For the reasons recorded hereinabove, these
petitions, along with the connected petitions, are disposed
of in the following terms;
I. Although every tehsil became a rating
area by operation of Section 44(1) of the Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa Local Government Act, 2013, the
levy, assessment and recovery of Urban
Immovable Property Tax nevertheless remained
subject to fulfilment of the mandatory
requirements prescribed under Sections 42(2)
and 44(2) of the said Act.
II. The power to approve or determine rates
under Section 44(2) of the Act of 2013 is
legislative or, at the very least, quasi-legislative
in character and has been expressly vested by
the Legislature in the competent Tehsil Council.
Such authority could neither be assumed nor
25
lawfully exercised by administrative officers
functioning under Section 120-A of the Act of
2013 in the absence of any express statutory
authorization.
III. The continuity contemplated by Section
44(3) extends only to rates lawfully operative in
areas previously subjected to Urban Immovable
Property Tax in accordance with law and
cannot be interpreted so as to defeat or nullify
the statutory exemption expressly created by the
proviso to Section 44(2) in respect of areas
where no lawful determination or approval of
rates has been made by the competent authority.
IV. Consequently, all notifications, orders,
approvals, determinations or other instruments
issued by any authorized officer or
administrative functionary purporting to
approve, determine, revise or impose the rates
of Urban Immovable Property Tax without the
prior approval of the competent Tehsil Council
are hereby declared to be without lawful
authority, coram non judice and of no legal
effect. As a necessary consequence thereof, all
assessments, PT-10 Forms, PT-11 Forms,
demand notices, final notices, recovery notices
and all other consequential proceedings
impugned in these petitions, having been issued
26
pursuant to and founded upon such
notifications, are hereby set aside. The
respondents shall, however, remain at liberty to
proceed afresh for the levy, assessment and
recovery of Urban Immovable Property Tax
strictly in accordance with law, after due
compliance with all mandatory statutory
requirements envisaged under Sections 42 and
44 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local
Government Act, 2013, as well as all other
relevant provisions governing the imposition,
assessment and recovery of the said tax.

headnote:
(a) Section 44 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government Act, 2013
establishes a complete statutory framework for the levy and recovery of Urban
Immovable Property Tax. While every tehsil is deemed to be a rating area, the
imposition of property tax is not automatic. Section 44(2) expressly requires
that the applicable rate of tax be determined and approved by the respective
Tehsil Council. The proviso further provides that where no rate has been
determined, the concerned area shall be deemed exempt from property tax
until such determination is made. Section 44(3) merely preserves continuity of
rates that were already lawfully operative and cannot be interpreted in a
manner that nullifies the requirement of approval by the Tehsil Council or the
statutory exemption created by the proviso. The provision must be read as a cohesive whole. The declaration of a tehsil
as a rating area only identifies the territorial scope of taxation; it does not by
itself create an enforceable tax liability. Unless the rate is lawfully determined
and approved by the competent authority, no valid assessment, demand, or
recovery of Urban Immovable Property Tax can be sustained. Any contrary
interpretation would render the proviso and the role assigned to the Tehsil
Council redundant, contrary to settled principles of statutory interpretation. (b) The power to determine and approve property tax rates under Sections 42
and 44 is not a purely administrative function. Although local governments do
not possess plenary legislative powers comparable to Parliament or Provincial
Assemblies, they may exercise delegated or quasi-legislative powers
expressly conferred by statute. The determination of tax rates directly affects
the proprietary and financial rights of citizens and is therefore legislative or, at
the very least, quasi-legislative in character. The statutory scheme entrusts this authority to elected local councils because
taxation decisions involve public accountability, democratic representation,
and fiscal policy considerations. Section 42(2) further reinforces this position
by requiring prior publication of proposals, consideration of objections, and
approval by the local council before any tax can be levied. These safeguards
are substantive requirements intended to ensure transparency, participation,
and lawful exercise of taxing powers. Consequently, the determination or
approval of tax rates cannot be treated as a routine administrative act capable
of being exercised by executive functionaries. (c) The contention that administrative officers could exercise the powers of
Tehsil Councils under Section 120-A of the Act was rejected. Section 120-A
was enacted as a transitional provision to ensure continuity of local
administration during periods when elected local governments were not
functioning. Its purpose was limited to facilitating day-to-day administration
and maintaining local governance during the transitional period.
The power to levy, determine, or approve taxes is fundamentally legislative
and financial in nature and cannot be assumed by administrative officers in
the absence of clear and express statutory authorization. Interpreting Section
120-A as transferring such powers to executive officers would undermine the
constitutional scheme of democratic local government and render the
statutory role of elected councils ineffective. Administrative officers could
therefore perform routine administrative functions but could not lawfully
exercise legislative or fiscal powers specifically reserved for representative
local institutions. Accordingly, although every tehsil constituted a rating area under Section
44(1), the levy, assessment, and recovery of Urban Immovable Property Tax
remained subject to strict compliance with Sections 42 and 44 of the Act.
Since the determination and approval of tax rates had not been carried out by
the competent Tehsil Councils, all notifications, approvals, assessments,
demand notices, recovery notices, and related proceedings issued by
administrative officers were held to be without lawful authority and were set
aside. Nevertheless, the authorities were permitted to initiate fresh
proceedings in accordance with law after complying with all mandatory
statutory requirements.
